js_lesson_1.title: Welcome to JavaScript
js_lesson_1.description: Your first steps into the world of web programming

js_lesson_1:slide:0.title: What is JavaScript? 🌐
js_lesson_1:slide:0.content:
JavaScript is the programming language of the web! It makes websites interactive and dynamic.

Every website you visit uses JavaScript:
• Animations and effects
• Form validation
• Interactive maps
• Games and apps

It's one of the most popular languages in the world!

js_lesson_1:slide:1.title: JavaScript Everywhere
js_lesson_1:slide:1.content:
JavaScript started as a browser language, but now it runs everywhere!

🌐 Frontend: React, Vue, Angular
⚙️ Backend: Node.js, Express
📱 Mobile: React Native
🖥️ Desktop: Electron
🎮 Games: Phaser, Three.js

js_lesson_1:slide:2.title: Your First JavaScript
js_lesson_1:slide:2.content: Let's write your first JavaScript code! We use console.log() to display messages.

js_lesson_1:question:0.explanation: JavaScript is the language of the web, making websites dynamic and interactive!

js_lesson_1:question:1.prompt: Which function displays output in JavaScript?
js_lesson_1:question:1.explanation: console.log() is the standard way to output messages in JavaScript.

js_lesson_1:question:2.explanation: JavaScript runs everywhere - in browsers (frontend), on servers with Node.js, and even in mobile/desktop apps!

js_lesson_1:question:3.explanation: JavaScript was created by Brendan Eich at Netscape in 1995 in just 10 days!

js_lesson_1:question:4.explanation: Each lesson objective is to build practical skill with one focused concept.

js_lesson_2.title: Variables - Storing Data
js_lesson_2.description: Learn how to store and use information in JavaScript

js_lesson_2:slide:0.title: What are Variables? 📦
js_lesson_2:slide:0.content:
Variables are containers for storing data. Think of them as labeled boxes where you can put information.

In JavaScript, we have three ways to create variables:
• let - for values that change
• const - for values that stay the same
• var - the old way (avoid using)

js_lesson_2:slide:1.title: Creating Variables
js_lesson_2:slide:1.content: Here's how to create and use variables:

js_lesson_2:slide:2.title: Data Types
js_lesson_2:slide:2.content:
JavaScript has several data types:

📝 String: "Hello" (text in quotes)
🔢 Number: 42, 3.14 (numbers)
✅ Boolean: true, false
📋 Array: [1, 2, 3] (lists)
📦 Object: {name: "Alex"} (complex data)

js_lesson_2:question:0.prompt: Which keyword creates a variable that cannot be changed?
js_lesson_2:question:0.explanation: const creates constants - values that cannot be reassigned.

js_lesson_2:question:1.explanation: Text in quotes is called a String in JavaScript.

js_lesson_2:question:2.prompt: What happens if you use a variable before declaring it with let?
js_lesson_2:question:2.explanation: With let, variables are not hoisted like var. Accessing them before declaration causes a ReferenceError (temporal dead zone).

js_lesson_2:question:3.prompt: Which statement about const is true?
js_lesson_2:question:3.explanation: const prevents reassignment of the variable, but if it's an object or array, the contents can still be modified!

options.js_lesson_2:question:3:option:0: The value can never be modified

js_lesson_2:question:4.explanation: This is a famous JavaScript quirk! typeof null returns "object" - a bug that can't be fixed due to backward compatibility.

js_lesson_3.title: Operators - Math & Logic
js_lesson_3.description: Learn to perform calculations and comparisons

js_lesson_3:slide:0.title: Math Operators ➕
js_lesson_3:slide:0.content:
JavaScript can do math! Here are the basic operators:

+ Addition
- Subtraction
* Multiplication
/ Division
% Modulus (remainder)
** Exponentiation (power)

js_lesson_3:slide:2.title: Comparison Operators
js_lesson_3:slide:2.content:
Compare values to get true or false:

== Equal value
=== Equal value AND type
!= Not equal
> Greater than
< Less than
>= Greater or equal
<= Less or equal

js_lesson_3:question:0.explanation: The modulus operator returns the remainder. 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2.

js_lesson_3:question:1.explanation: === checks both value AND type. "5" === 5 is false!

js_lesson_3:question:2.explanation: JavaScript coerces the number to a string and concatenates them, resulting in "55". This is type coercion in action!

js_lesson_3:question:3.prompt: Which operator would you use to check if two values are NOT equal in type AND value?
js_lesson_3:question:3.explanation: !== is the strict inequality operator. It returns true if values differ in value OR type.

js_lesson_3:question:4.explanation: Each lesson objective is to build practical skill with one focused concept.

js_lesson_4:slide:0.title: Strings - Text Data 📝
js_lesson_4:slide:0.content:
Strings are text values. You can create them with:

• Single quotes: 'Hello'
• Double quotes: "Hello"
• Backticks: `Hello` (template literals)

Backticks are special - they allow embedding variables!

js_lesson_4:slide:1.title: Template Literals
js_lesson_4:slide:1.content: Template literals let you embed expressions:

js_lesson_4:slide:2.title: String Methods
js_lesson_4:slide:2.content:
Strings have useful methods:

.length - get length
.toUpperCase() - UPPERCASE
.toLowerCase() - lowercase
.includes() - check if contains
.slice() - extract part

js_lesson_4:question:1.explanation: toUpperCase() converts all letters to uppercase.

js_lesson_4:question:2.prompt: What is the output of: `The answer is 8`?
js_lesson_4:question:2.explanation: Template literals (backticks) evaluate expressions inside ${}. So 5 + 3 becomes 8.

js_lesson_4:question:3.prompt: How do you get the length of a string "hello"?
js_lesson_4:question:3.explanation: .length is a property (not a method), so no parentheses are needed. "hello".length returns 5.

js_lesson_4:question:4.explanation: slice(0, 4) extracts characters from index 0 to 3 (end index is exclusive), returning "Java".

js_lesson_5.title: If Statements - Making Decisions
js_lesson_5.description: Learn to write code that makes choices

js_lesson_5:slide:0.title: Conditional Logic 🤔
js_lesson_5:slide:0.content:
Programs need to make decisions! If statements let your code choose different paths based on conditions.

Think of it like: "IF it's raining, THEN take umbrella, ELSE wear sunglasses"

js_lesson_5:slide:1.title: If Statement Syntax
js_lesson_5:slide:1.content: Here's how to write if statements:

js_lesson_5:slide:2.title: Multiple Conditions

js_lesson_5:question:1.prompt: If x = 5, what does (x > 3) evaluate to?
js_lesson_5:question:1.explanation: 5 is greater than 3, so the condition is true.

js_lesson_5:question:2.prompt: What is the purpose of the else if statement?
js_lesson_5:question:2.explanation: else if allows you to test multiple conditions in order. The first true condition executes, then the rest are skipped.

js_lesson_6.title: Working with Arrays
js_lesson_6.description: Master JavaScript arrays and their methods

js_lesson_6:slide:0.title: What are Arrays? 📚
js_lesson_6:slide:0.content:
Arrays store multiple values in a single variable. They are ordered and can hold any data type.

Common uses:
• User lists
• Shopping carts
• Playlists
• Game scores

js_lesson_6:slide:1.title: Creating Arrays
js_lesson_6:slide:1.content: Arrays use square brackets with comma-separated values.

js_lesson_6:question:0.prompt: Which method adds an element to the end?
js_lesson_6:question:0.explanation: push() adds elements to the end of an array.

js_lesson_6:question:1.prompt: How do you access the first element?
js_lesson_6:question:1.explanation: Arrays are zero-indexed, so arr[0] is the first element.

js_lesson_6:question:2.prompt: What does the spread operator (...) do with arrays?
js_lesson_6:question:2.explanation: The spread operator (...) expands array elements. Example: [...arr1, ...arr2] combines two arrays.

js_lesson_6:question:3.explanation: Destructuring unpacks array values: const [a, b] = [1, 2] assigns a=1, b=2. It's a clean way to extract values!

js_lesson_6:question:4.explanation: filter() creates a new array with elements that pass the test. Only 2 and 3 are greater than 1.

js_lesson_7:question:2.prompt: What is the key difference between for...of and for...in?

js_lesson_8:slide:0.title: What are Objects? 🏷️
js_lesson_8:slide:0.content:
Objects store data as key-value pairs (properties). They represent real-world entities.

Examples:
• User profiles
• Product details
• Game characters
• Configuration settings

js_lesson_8:slide:1.title: Creating Objects
js_lesson_8:slide:1.content: Objects use curly braces with property: value pairs.

js_lesson_8:slide:3.title: Object Manipulation
js_lesson_8:slide:3.content: Add, update, or delete properties dynamically.

js_lesson_8:question:0.prompt: How do you access object properties?
js_lesson_8:question:0.explanation: Use dot notation or bracket notation to access properties.

js_lesson_8:question:1.prompt: What is "this" in an object method?

js_lesson_9:slide:0.title: Function Basics 📦
js_lesson_9:slide:0.content: Functions are reusable blocks of code. JavaScript has multiple ways to define them.

js_lesson_9:slide:3.title: Higher-Order Functions

js_lesson_9:question:0.prompt: What is the syntax for arrow functions?

js_lesson_9:question:1.prompt: What does the map() method do?
js_lesson_9:question:1.explanation: map() creates a new array by transforming each element.

js_lesson_9:question:2.prompt: What is a closure in JavaScript?
js_lesson_9:question:2.explanation: A closure is when a function "remembers" variables from its outer scope, even after that scope has finished executing!

options.js_lesson_9:question:2:option:0: A way to close a function

js_lesson_9:question:3.prompt: What is the difference between function declarations and arrow functions regarding "this"?
js_lesson_9:question:3.explanation: Arrow functions inherit "this" from their surrounding scope (lexical this). Regular functions create their own "this" context.

js_lesson_9:question:4.prompt: What does the reduce() method do?
js_lesson_9:question:4.explanation: reduce() executes a reducer function on each element, resulting in a single output value. Example: sum all numbers.

js_lesson_10.title: Asynchronous JavaScript
js_lesson_10.description: Handle timing, promises, and async operations

js_lesson_10:slide:0.title: What is Async? ⏱️
js_lesson_10:slide:0.content:
Asynchronous code doesn't wait for operations to complete. It continues running and handles results later.

Common async operations:
• Network requests
• File reading
• Database queries
• Timers

js_lesson_10:slide:1.title: Callbacks
js_lesson_10:slide:1.content: The original way to handle async operations.

js_lesson_10:slide:2.title: Promises
js_lesson_10:slide:2.content: Modern way to handle async operations. A promise represents a future value.

js_lesson_10:slide:3.title: Async/Await
js_lesson_10:slide:3.content: The cleanest syntax for async code. Makes it read like synchronous code.

js_lesson_10:question:0.explanation: setTimeout() delays code execution by a specified time.

js_lesson_10:question:1.prompt: What keyword makes a function async?
js_lesson_10:question:1.explanation: The async keyword makes a function asynchronous.

js_lesson_10:question:2.explanation: await pauses async function execution until the promise resolves, making async code look synchronous. Only works inside async functions!

js_lesson_10:question:3.prompt: What are the three states of a Promise?
js_lesson_10:question:3.explanation: A Promise can be pending (initial), fulfilled (successful), or rejected (failed). Use .then() for fulfilled and .catch() for rejected.

js_lesson_10:question:4.explanation: Promise.all() runs multiple promises concurrently and resolves when ALL complete (or rejects if ANY fails). Great for parallel operations!

options.js_lesson_10:question:4:option:0: Running promises one at a time
